title: In an AI-assisted development world, how much implementation detail should indie developers make public?
author: RedTowerDev
selftext:
I’ve been thinking about how much of our development process I should actually be making public now that AI is getting better at turning descriptions into working systems.  
We make fairly detailed patch notes for Nine Thrones, and lately I’ve started wondering whether I’m giving away more than I should.  
I’m not particularly worried about somebody copying the basic idea of the game. Ideas are cheap, and most of what makes the game work is how everything fits together.  
What I’m more unsure about is implementation detail.  
If I publicly explain enough about how our NPC memory, world simulation, faction systems, persistence, etc. work, at some point somebody can potentially just feed all of that into an AI and say “build me something like this.”  
A few years ago I probably wouldn’t have worried much about that because actually recreating it would still have been a huge engineering job. That gap is getting smaller pretty quickly.  
At the same time, detailed devlogs and patch notes are useful for players and other developers, and I don’t really want to become secretive about everything we’re building.  
Where are other people drawing that line now?  
Are you still publishing detailed technical information, or are you starting to keep the underlying implementation private and mostly talk about player-facing results?

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: in regards to if its ai or not, yoiu just need to follow store or other guidelines the rest is up to you. games like factorio satisfactories and other are partially popular because they share alot of how it works. go look at the decomp and recomp subs, they just need your game to remake it, you sharing anyhting won't do anything. other then make it look like your not hiding anyhting. llms right now are pretty good at making clones of existing products as well, they just need to analyze your game if enough written in text to copy it anyway.

comments.author: SlightOfHand_
comments.body:
The truth is, very soon you won’t be able to rely on security-through-obscurity anymore. Even if you chose to withhold patch notes, as long as your code is out, it can be reverse-engineered.

I think it makes sense to be as open as you’ve ever been, under the circumstances; the benefits are largely the same.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
It’s a really tricky subject that is evolving really quickly. I don’t think there is really anything that will be safe from AI duplication soon. Expect your game to get a free launch in China, whether you want it or not.

So what do we try and keep as our unique value, our moat? In product terms this is what sets you apart from the competition. What is it that you are selling.

For me it is my reference material and how I have chosen to combine it and extract value from it. I’m not expecting to sell my games for much if anything. I’m more interested in showing how I can work to a potential future employer.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
...I don't know this for sure, but I suspect what will happen is that decompiling will join CSAM generation and bioweapon research in the 'censored, and if you're caught doing it, you're banned' category. So what's happening now probably won't continue to happen

It's not in the interest of the people developing or funding LLMs for suddenly every piece of software to be open source.

  
In any case, I don't think the people who are decompiling and stealing things are going to be interested in 'reverse engineering' a description of a game when they can just steal a demo, open it up, add a couple of features and then put it up for sale. 

So I might cool it on demo publishing for a while (as bad as that is), and not worry too much about other material.

comments.author: ThreeDMK
comments.body:
There is very little value in the code we right, the products we deliver, or the documentation we create.

The value is in the minds of people who can create these things from nothing.  Anyone could feasibly use my development harness.  They won’t be nearly as effective and efficient as I am though.  This is a bespoke system.  It’s tailored to how I work.  

I share my code and ideas with people all the time.  If it helps them to be efficient and do more, that’s awesome.  I don’t have an attachment to these things like I used to.  I am hurler going to rebuild it all better 3-6 months from now.  ;)

replies.author: RedTowerDev
replies.body:
I think there’s a lot of truth to this. The real advantage is knowing what to build and how to bring everything together, instead of any particular piece of code.  
But I do think there’s a difference between sharing ideas and handing someone a detailed blueprint. We’re building some fairly interconnected systems in our RPG, and while I’m happy to discuss what we’re doing, I’m becoming a little more selective about publishing exactly how everything works.

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
I thought about this too, before AI game developers loved to share technical and implementation details with each other!

I think this will slowly stop. There is no reason to share clever implementation, architecture, design with others, because at the end it will just get fed in to AI or people will just prompt AI to do it. 

Before having talks and sharing information was about making others better and get a good name for a company etc.
